_source: docs/design/12-ui-ux.md §8 (Draft v1, report 98 amendments C-25/C-35/C-59/C-62/C-63/C-64/C-65/C-71/C-72/G-8). Transcribed verbatim; no number invented here.
_units: Every length is dp (Android density-independent pixels, doc 12 §2.1) unless the key says _m (metres) or _s / _ms (time).

layout._corner_rail_margin_dp: D-46. The bottom-right rail is the mirror of the left one: the incident drawer's handle is the tab and keeps the edge, and the alerts chip then the event-log chip stack in the column beside it, `rail_gap_dp` apart, each slot as tall as the chips measure. This is where the LOWEST chip's bottom edge sits, measured up from the safe area. 92 reproduces the scene's authored offsets exactly at 100 % text with 48 dp targets, so the reference box does not move.
layout._unlock_pulse_s: §2.13's progression payoff: how long a build card that a new city level just unlocked pulses for, once. A8 suppresses it entirely under reduce_motion — the toast still announces the level.
layout._top_bar_max_rows: §2.4's collapse solver hides P5-P7 once demotion runs out. On a near-square display (Fold inner, 2160x1856) the four never-hidden chips plus a measured value string still overflow one 48 dp row, and A1/A2 forbid clipping — so the bar wraps to a second row BEFORE anything is hidden. 1 restores the doc's single-row behaviour exactly.
layout._goal_chip_index: S14 (doc 09 §2.14, doc 12 §2.19). Where HudModel inserts the goal chip into `chip_priority` while the curriculum is unfinished. 1 puts it immediately after the treasury — the reading a goal most often costs money against — and inside §2.4's never-hidden prefix, which the solver widens by one to compensate. The chip is deliberately NOT a row of `chip_priority`, because it RETIRES when the curriculum is done: a teaching surface may not cost the reference layout a permanent demotion.
layout._population_flash_s: D-100 (report 98 RR-203). How long the population chip pulses when the number in it MOVES. Doc 01 settles population once per game-hour, so a house the player placed changes the chip in ONE jump up to 176 real seconds after the tap — long enough that the player is looking somewhere else, which is the whole of the 2026-09-04 report. Same mechanism and the same 1.2 Hz as Wave 14's deposit pulse, and A8 suppresses it with every other pulse. 0 turns it off.

goals._comment: S14 (doc 12 §2.19) — the goals SHEET's own tunables. The curriculum itself is data/goals.json (doc 09 §8.3) and nothing about it lives here.
goals._max_reward_rows: How many lines the reward card prints before it stops. The lines are READ — the celebration grant, build cards, the upgrade tier, land — so a rung that happens to open nine things would otherwise push the objectives off a 360 dp display. 4 → 5 in Wave 22 (doc 92 §61): the grant line is NEW and it prints FIRST, so leaving the cap at 4 would have silently dropped an unlock line that used to print. The number of UNLOCK lines the card can show is unchanged at four.

_comment_states: Exactly four data states — these four ARE doc 11's 2-bit overlay_state (C-64). SELECTED is not one of them.

overlay._strip_chip_dp: 64 dp clipped `Power` to `Powe` and `Traffic` to `Traffi` — A1/A2 forbid clipping, and a console whose labels are truncated teaches the player nothing. 104 dp fits the longest mode name at the 1.0 text scale with the theme's own margins; the strip widened to match (game/ui/ui_root.tscn).
overlay._enabled_modes: An overlay ships enabled only once the sim behind it publishes an OverlayQuery (doc 12 §4.4). All six are live as of Wave 5: POWER (doc 04), WATER (doc 05 §5.8 + WaterSystem.service_factors), TRAFFIC (doc 10 §2.15's TrafficSnapshot) and now POLICE/FIRE (doc 02 §2.9's coverage field, C-51, published by CityIncidentWorld.coverage_police/coverage_fire). The greying machinery stays — A14 wants a blocked chip to state its reason in words rather than disappear — so pulling a system out of a build is still an edit to this array and nothing else.
overlay._shader_global: doc 11 reads the active overlay from this project shader global; its value is the mode's INDEX INTO overlay.modes above (none 0, power 1, water 2, police 3, fire 4, traffic 5). The int is written by ui/overlay_rail.gd and by nothing else; the per-instance 2-bit overlay_state that the building shader tints with is doc 11's and is never set from here (C-64).
overlay._water_bands: WATER (mode 2) is a per-BUILDING read: doc 05's service factor / delivered pressure on [0,1] becomes one of the four §2.5 data states, which doc 11 already carries as the 2-bit overlay_state packed in the instance buffer (C-64). First row whose `max` the value is at or below wins, so the rows must stay sorted ascending. `offline` is the honest answer for a tap with no water at all, not a dark red `critical`.
overlay._coverage_bands: POLICE (mode 3) and FIRE (mode 4) are per-BUILDING reads of doc 02 §2.9's coverage field (C-51) and ride the same 2-bit overlay_state WATER does. Two ladders, because doc 02 §2.9 says `the UI must show the margin, not just pass/fail`: a building whose level carries a coverage REQUIREMENT is banded on how it stands against that requirement (below it = its upgrades are blocked and it is paying the safety penalty, so CRITICAL), and one with no requirement — every L1, and every service/utility shell at low level — is banded on the absolute scalar. `coverage_margin_warn` is how much clear air above the requirement still reads as WARNING: 0.10 is a little more than one dispatched engine costs a two-engine station (doc 02 worked example E6 loses 0.31 outright), so a building inside it is one bad hour from failing its own gate.
overlay._legend_card: Doc 12 §2.5's OverlayLegend: a 200 dp card at the TOP-LEFT, under the top bar, carrying the overlay's name, its state rows and 1-3 aggregate lines. It replaces the legend that used to live inside the chip strip — the strip is a control, the legend is a reading, and the two do not belong in one panel (the strip also closes, which took the legend with it). Collapsible to a pill; `collapsed_modes` is the persisted set, per overlay, and lives in the `ui` save section beside `overlay`/`overlay_last`.
overlay._traffic_bands: TRAFFIC (mode 5) is a per-EDGE read, so it tints the ROAD, never the building. The five bands and their cut points are doc 10 §2.15's own (RoadCosts.overlay_band) and tests/test_ui_overlays.gd asserts the two tables agree — change one and the other fails. Colour is never load-bearing (constitution §11 / spec §49): `state` picks the hue out of the SAME palette the legend uses (so a colourblind variant carries it), `darken` deepens it, `alpha` is a monotone lightness ramp, and `stripe_duty` is a diagonal hatch whose density rises with congestion — the pattern channel that survives greyscale. `pulse_hz` is motion, reserved for the two bands that mean STOP.
overlay._building_state_paint: The colours the BUILDING overlay tints with, so the colourblind palette reaches the 3D city and not just the legend beside it (the road bands already did, via road_overlay_view). `hue` names a palette token — resolved through data/ui.json.palette[variant], which is exactly what the legend row is painted with, so a deuteran city and a deuteran legend can never disagree. `mix` is how far the albedo is pulled to that hue and `emission` how hard it glows; both are the building shader's own `overlay_normal_blend` / `overlay_data_blend` / `overlay_state_emission` split, restated per state so NORMAL can stay calm. NORMAL deliberately does NOT take the palette's green: a city where every healthy building glows is a city where nothing reads, so it borrows `text_dim` — a cool neutral — and only the three states that mean LOOK HERE carry hue. OFFLINE takes §2.5's own `#5A6270` — the shader shipped a dark RED there, which reads as an emergency when the honest meaning is `nothing to report from here`: on the coverage overlays every lot outside a station's reach is OFFLINE, and a city painted crisis-red end to end tells the player nothing. Grey is what the §2.5 state table says and what the legend row beside it is painted in.

alerts._comment: The §2.15 alerts centre: PRESENTATION ONLY. `events` is DELETED (2026-08-19) — the stand-in event→notification map moved wholesale to doc 08's data/notifications.json, which owns classes, priorities, budgets and quiet hours (report C-71) and is what ui/alerts_model.gd now reads. Class and surface still come from in_app_alerts above (C-71/C-72). Nothing in this block decides what the player is told; it decides how wide the panel is.

construction._comment: S16 (doc 12 §2.22) — the construction queue: PRESENTATION ONLY. Not one number in this block is a price, a duration or a rate; every one of those belongs to doc 03 and reaches this screen through CitySim.construction_overview()'s `rush_cost` and `eta_gm`. What is here is the width of a column, the height of a row and the length of a flash, which is all a view is allowed to own.
construction._bar_h_dp: The per-row progress bar. Thinner than S14's level bar (10) and thicker than §2.6's escalation clock (4): this one is read at a glance down a column of four, so it wants weight without becoming the row.
construction._chip_flash_s: How long the treasury chip pulses after a rush is paid for — the same beat §2.21's payday uses, and deliberately the same number, because a dollar leaving and a dollar arriving must not feel like two different mechanisms.

event_log._comment: S13 (doc 12) — the city's HISTORY. The alerts centre above is a to-do list that coalesces and is marked read; this is the ledger behind it: one row per event, newest first, filtered by category, never coalesced and never persisted (§3.2 keeps no feed in the save — a resumed city starts its log from the resume). Copy resolves the SAME `n_<notify_id>_title`/`_body` keys the alerts centre and doc 13's pushes use, so a line in the log and the push that woke the player can never drift (G-8). `category` is the only thing this table adds that `alerts.events` does not have, and it is the whole filter strip.
event_log._recent_minutes: Below this many game-minutes a row reads `just now` rather than `0 min ago`.

events._comment: Doc 05's diagnostic half, logged — doc 91 §18.2's named exception, closed. Seven rows and four sentences: the three `*_failed` types share one notify_id because a failed pump, plant and source are the same sentence and the same job. `water_tank_low` is here and NOT in data/notifications.json: a tank drawing on reserve belongs in the ledger, not on a lock screen.

NEW, Wave 21 (doc 93 sec AS1, doc 12 D-94). The harsher of a fire's two terminal outcomes, and it had never been on the feed at all: doc 06 has emitted `building_destroyed_by_fire` since Wave 8 and no router named it, so a building the fire actually TOOK was announced only by doc 02's own `building_destroyed`, which says nothing about a fire. Its sibling row below is the other ending. Both, or neither -- a feed that could only say one of them is how the 3,891 lying events in doc 92 sec 60.3 went unnoticed for a wave.

NEW, Wave 21 (doc 93 sec AS1, doc 12 D-94). The other half of a fire's terminal outcome. Under sec AS1 a city with no fire service gets its building CONDEMNED rather than destroyed, and until this row the feed could only ever say the harsher sentence -- `incident_failed`, `it burned out`, about a building that is still standing. It sits beside that row on purpose: same fire, same moment, different ending, and the player has to be able to tell which one they got, because one of them has a REPAIR button behind it (doc 12 D-94).

The rung BEFORE the collapse. Doc 10 latches this once per tile as the surface runs out, and it was read by tests only — so the only warning a player ever had that a road was about to fail was the road failing. Log-only and deliberately: it is a maintenance job, not a lock-screen event, and `key: tile` gives the row a camera jump the shell's locator already resolves.

The other half of austerity, and of the relief that pays for it. `austerity_entered` was announced and `austerity_exited` was read by tests only, so the game told the player when the belt tightened and never when it came off; `relief_grant_awarded` is money arriving in the treasury that nothing anywhere mentioned. Both are log-only — the budget sheet is where a player goes to argue with numbers, and neither is worth a push.

report 98 RR-79. The LOG carries the celebration grant and the push does not: city_level_up already wakes the player for that moment, and a second push for the same rung would be the game repeating itself. A payment, though, belongs in the money ledger — this is the row that makes the grant a thing the player can find again an hour later.

99-PA PA-32 / doc 98 RR-148. Doc 03 §2.5a's founding assistance retires $589.71 a game-day for seven game-days and used to do it in total silence: the audit measured it as the largest single mover of the opening fortnight's net chip, with no toast, no log row and no end date anywhere, and named that silence as most of what reads on the phone as 'income too slow'. `EconomySystem` now steps the grant out loud once per game-day. TWO rows because the last step is a different sentence: days 0-6 are `final: false` and are routine bookkeeping the player can scroll back to, while day 7 is `final: true`, is the day the city starts paying its own departments and fleet, and is the ONE that is also a doc 08 notification (see data/notifications.json). Exactly 8 rows per city, then never again.

99-PA PA-31 / doc 98 RR-149. Doc 02 §2.6's two band lines, in the log, one row per crossing — the log's own rule (§S13: never coalesced, because the third one is the interesting one). The ALERTS centre is where these aggregate into 'N buildings are wearing out'; here they are the ledger behind that number, filed under `economy` because what a worn building costs is money and not maintenance trivia, and keyed on `building` so a Poor row carries `Jump to it`.

NEW, Wave 19 (doc 93 §AP1, doc 12 D-88). The fourth band, and the only TERMINAL one: §AP1 stops wear demolishing private stock, so a building that reaches the structural-failure line now rests there instead of disappearing. It is filed under `economy` beside its three siblings for their reason — what a condemned building costs is money — and keyed on `building` so the row carries `Jump to it`, which matters more here than for Worn or Poor because the fix is at the building (its power), not in a menu.

99-PA PA-83. Land development charges the treasury SIX times per block, $1.2K to $21K a phase, 14-15 times per 21 game-days on a curriculum run, and until now not one of them appeared anywhere the player could see: `development_phase_charged` had zero shell consumers. A log row and nothing louder — the player pressed DEVELOP and the schedule is doc 03 §2.8's own, so this is a receipt, not news. `phase` resolves through the same `ui_land_phase_*` copy the land panel's own progress line uses, because 'road_install started on Block E4' is a sentence written by a machine for a machine.

99-PA PA-33 / doc 98 RR-150. The auto-repair pass's receipt. `count` is the PAYLOAD's own number, not `@count`: one pass repaired N buildings, and the log row for that pass has to say N rather than 1.

Doc 07 §2.4's flood, logged (defect A91-D-26). The four rows below are the whole of what a ledger should carry about standing water, and the rule that picked them is written out in data/notifications.json's `_comment_flood`: NARRATE the bands that change what the player can do, DRAW the ones that only change how the street looks. So 100 mm (vehicles start stalling) and 200 mm (civilian traffic is turned back) are here, 40 mm is not, and the all-clear is `road_reopened` rather than `flood_level_changed{band: dry}` — `dry` fires after any shower at all, `road_reopened` fires only for a cell that was actually shut. `key: cell` gives the row an identity to coalesce on and, once the shell's locator learns the key shape, something to jump to; a locator that cannot place it simply offers no jump.

The storm CELL's own arc (doc 07 §2.7.1). `weather_changed` says the sky turned; this says the cell that carries the strikes arrived over the city and later left it, which is a different fact and the one that decides whether a transformer is about to be hit. Two rows, matched on the phase, because `peak` and `trailing` are pacing internals the player has no verb for.

Wave 19 — doc 03 §2.5b's commissions board (report 98 §60 RR-170). FOUR rows and not seven: `contract_accepted` and `contract_progress` are the player's own tap, and the band they tapped it on is already showing them; `contract_withdrawn` is an offer nobody took. These four are the ones that happen while the player is looking somewhere else, which is doc 93's own test for whether an event owes the log a line. `client` resolves through `@lookup:` with an EMPTY prefix because the payload already carries a string-table key rather than a bare id — the board is authored in `data/contracts.json` and its copy is authored in the string table, and the event is the one place the two meet.

incident_drawer._comment: S6 (doc 12 §2.6). The drawer's GEOMETRY is already in `layout` (drawer_w_ratio/min/max, drawer_row_h_dp, drawer_handle_dp, drawer_handle_center_from_bottom_dp, drawer_anim_s) and its escalation-bar thresholds are already in `thresholds` (escalation_bar_critical_remaining_tiers, escalation_bar_held_when_assist_ratio_ge) — this block adds only what §2.6 says and no other block does: the sort orders, the row cap, and the two glyph sets.
incident_drawer._max_rows: The drawer is a list of things to DO, not a log; doc 06's storm cascade can open dozens at once and a list past this depth is not readable on a phone. The lowest-tier row is the one dropped, never a T5.
incident_drawer._tier_glyphs: §2.6's A5 redundancy set, verbatim: T1 ▪, T2 ▴, T3 ▴▴, T4 ◆, T5 ✶. The tier DIGIT is the primary channel; these reinforce it. Colours are palette.tier1…tier5, which already exist.
incident_drawer._kind_glyphs: One per doc 06 incident `type`. Keys are doc 06's type ids verbatim so a rename there is a visible miss here rather than a silent fallback.

unit_picker._comment: S7 (doc 12 §2.6 steps 1-5). Sheet height and row height are `layout.unit_picker_h_dp` / `layout.unit_row_h_dp`; the rank key is §2.6's and lives in ui/unit_picker_model.gd. This block carries only the department glyph set — doc 06 owns the department names.

dashboard._comment: S8 (doc 12 §2.10). All four tabs are live as of Wave 5: Infrastructure reads PowerGrid.feeder_rows/transformer_rows/capacity_summary (doc 04) and WaterSnapshot's §5.8 zones (doc 05); Response reads FleetSystem's roster plus DispatchSystem.stats (doc 06). Dropping a tab is still an edit to this array and nothing else.
dashboard._worst_n: §2.10 asks for `worst 5 feeders` and `worst 5 zones`. One number, because the two lists sit on one scrolling tab and a reader who can hold five rows of one can hold five of the other. The lists are sorted worst-first on load ratio (feeders/transformers) and lowest-pressure-first (zones), with the id as the tiebreak so the order never depends on hashing.
dashboard._response_departments: Doc 06 §2.11's five departments, in roster order. A department with no station in the city still prints its row — `0 of 0` is a reading, and a row that vanishes teaches the player that fire trucks are optional.
dashboard._response_target_min: The response time the rolling score is graded against (doc 06 §2.9's `target_response_min`). It is the UI's THRESHOLD, not the sim's: the score itself is DispatchSystem.stats.rolling_response_score and is computed there.
dashboard._series: What ui/history_model.gd rings. `power01`/`water01` are the [0,1] service fractions the ⚡/💧 chips read, sampled at the same hourly boundary as the rest.
dashboard._history_capacity: 168 hourly samples = 7 game-days, exactly what §2.10's '7-day treasury chart' needs. The ring is fixed-size and is NOT persisted: doc 12 §3.2 fixes the `ui` save section and report 98 §E2 makes save identity exact.

budget._comment: The Economy tab's ledger. Keys are doc 03's settle-snapshot keys VERBATIM (`revenue.*` and `expenses.*` from EconomySystem.settle_hour) so a rename there shows up as a missing line here rather than as a wrong total. Order is the reading order, not doc 03's; the tax ladder itself is doc 03's and is never restated here.
budget._comment_side_revenue: Wave 14 adds two keys doc 03 does not settle: `bounties` and `street`. They are DIRECT credits — `Treasury.credit(amount, &"incident", …)` from a resolved incident's reward, and the same door a collected street opportunity uses — so they never pass through `EconomySystem.settle_hour` and no row of this ledger has ever contained them. That is not a rounding error: one resolved structure fire pays $1,530, against $1,470 of power tariff + water tariff + fines per settled hour on this tab's own fixture, and until now the Economy tab's NET was wrong by exactly the bounty income every hour a crew answered a call. Until doc 03 settles them, `BudgetModel.feed_side_revenue()` supplies the two lines from the UI's own per-hour tally of the bus events that paid them, and the moment a settle snapshot carries either key the sim's number wins and the tally is ignored — so this retires itself rather than needing to be found again.

land._comment: S4 (doc 12 §2.8), the land purchase panel. PRESENTATION ONLY. The price is doc 03 §2.7's (EconomySystem.land_price), the phase costs are §2.8's, the six phases and their crew-hours are doc 09 §2.3's (DevelopmentController), and the block's own attributes are doc 09's starter-city data — none of them is restated here. What this block owns is which risks get a row, how a [0,1] risk becomes five segments and one word, and the glyphs the bars are drawn with.
land._risk_bands: Five words over [0,1], band = clamp(floor(v*5), 0, 4), so 0.00-0.19 is `low` and 0.80-1.00 is `severe`. The word and the bar both carry the reading (A5): colour is the third channel, never the only one, which is why `risk_band_states` has fewer distinct values than there are bands.
land._advantage_min_pct: §2.8's `advantages` are the terms of the price product, measured by re-pricing the block with each term neutralised (see ui/land_panel_model.gd). A term worth less than this either way is dropped: a `+0 %` row is noise, and rounding a real 0.4 % to `+0 %` is a lie about a number that is not zero.

street._comment: Wave 14's street life — the tap, not the characters (doc 11 owns those) and not the roster (the sim owns that). Four numbers, and every one of them is about the finger rather than about the economy: no reward, no spawn rate and no lifetime is authored here or anywhere else in ui/.
street._tap_dp: The pick radius, in dp, converted to metres at the CURRENT zoom before the roster is asked (BuildController.set_tap_radius_from). 48 is §2.1's touch target and the same number `marker_tap_dp` uses, on purpose: a loose dog is a 32 dp sprite, and a pick that demanded the exact pixel would make the most-tapped thing in the game the hardest thing to tap. It is spelled here rather than shared with `marker_tap_dp` because that one is a Control's minimum SIZE and this one is a world-space RADIUS — they agree today and there is no reason they must agree tomorrow.
street._coach_ttl_s: How long the one-time discovery mark stays up before it retires itself. It is not a tutorial step (gate 21 counts those and this is not one of them): it never gates, it never repeats, and if the player collects the thing first it comes down on the collect.
street._chip_flash_s: The treasury chip's deposit pulse, in real seconds, at §2.5's `state_pulse_hz.critical` rate. A8 suppresses the motion entirely — the toast and the ledger still carry the money.
street._toast_min: A bounty below this is not worth a toast: a $12 fender-bender clearing itself would otherwise interrupt the player once an hour to say so. The cue and the chip pulse still fire — they cost no attention — and the ledger still counts every dollar.

settings._comment: S9 (doc 12 §2.13), Phase-1 pages only. Every row is data so the sheet holds no option list and no default; `options_from`/`default_from` resolve against data/render.json (doc 11 owns the graphics presets) and this file's own `defaults` block.

rows._comment: D-75 / report 98 RR-126 — the refresh pin. The game caps Engine.max_fps at the preset's target_fps and had never DECLARED that rate to the display; on the reference device's 1-120 Hz LTPO panel the platform then infers a mode from cadence and hunts when the cadence changes, which is the banding the player reports in the sub menus. AUTO (the default) declares whatever the cap is; 60 and 120 pin the panel outright; OFF declares nothing and is the shipped behaviour, kept because the A/B needs a control arm that is the build rather than a rebuild of it. The ladder is doc 11's file (`render.json.refresh.settings_modes`), never a second copy here — 90 is on the LEVER and not on this row, because the reference panel has no 90 Hz mode for a player to land on. Device-scoped, like the preset above it.

§2.14. off / light / full, default light, durations in `haptics_ms` above. `reduce_motion` SUPPRESSES haptics without changing this row (A8: a vibration is motion), so switching reduce_motion back off restores the player's own choice.

S12's reset (doc 12 §2.17: the tutorial never shows again once done, unless the player asks for it here). Switching it ON restarts the coach flow from step 0 and the row switches itself back OFF — it is a door, not a preference, and it is per-city, so it is NOT in device_scoped_keys.

PA-58, Wave 18 — §2.13's GAMEPLAY block, which had defaults in this file and no rows and no readers. All three are per-CITY rather than device-scoped, and that is a judgement rather than an oversight: which way a camera pans and whether it chases an engine are habits a player forms on a phone, but `follow_dispatched_unit` in particular reads as a property of how they are playing THIS city, and doc 12 §3.2's device list names neither of the two. `rotation_mode` is doc 12's own four-value enum (CameraState.RotationMode); the ladder is inline because it IS the enum — an options_from pointing at a second copy of four constants would be the drift this file is written to avoid. `battery_saver` and confirm-before-demolish stay defaults-with-no-row and are recorded as DEFERRED in doc 12 §2.13; see that section for why each is not a row yet.

§2.13's AUTO-RESPONSE block (doc 06 §2.12, doc 91 D-11). Every row below carries `policy: dispatch`: its default is read from data/dispatch.json.policy_defaults — doc 06's own file, never a second copy here — and its value is written with CitySim.cmd_set_dispatch_policy, which refuses any key DispatchPolicy does not carry. The keys are spelled exactly as the sim spells them, so a row can never address a policy that does not exist. The utility RESTORATION ORDER (a drag-reorder list) is deliberately absent: it is a list, not a 48 dp cycling target, and shipping it as one would be a control that lies about what it does.
§2.13's `reserve N fire engines`. The ladder is the control's, the default is doc 06's; 3 is the top because a reserve larger than a starter station's roster would refuse every fire.
§2.13's `auto-repair cost ceiling`, whose stated range is $0-$250K. A cycling row rather than a drag slider (A3), so the range is a ladder; doc 06's default sits on it.

Doc 10 §2.13's AUTOMATIC ROAD REPAIR, the pair `RoadNetwork.cmd_set_auto_repair_policy` takes. Doc 93 §J3 rules road condition the policy's job rather than a per-tile player verb, which makes these two dials the whole of the player's say over it. Both carry `policy: roads`: the ladder and the default are read from data/roads.json.condition — doc 10's own file, never a second copy here — and a change writes the PAIR, because the command takes both at once. The threshold ladder is the sim's own `auto_repair_thresholds`, so a rung the command would answer E_BAD_THRESHOLD for can never appear on the control.

The daily spend cap, a cycling ladder rather than a drag slider (A3). $25,000 is doc 10's own `auto_repair_default_daily_cap` and sits on the ladder; $0 is `no automatic repair spending at all` and is why the row carries a `zero_key`.

Doc 11 §2.13's adaptive governor (game/render/perf_governor.gd). ON by default: the preset above is a ceiling the player picks, and this decides whether the game is allowed to spend less than it under load or thermal pressure. Switching it OFF freezes the knobs where they stand rather than snapping them back to the preset -- a quality JUMP at the moment the player asks for manual control is the one thing the toggle must not do. Device-scoped, like the preset it modulates.

S10 (doc 12 §2.13) — the notification rows. These are a VIEW of doc 08's policy, not a second copy of it: the master switch and the three class switches write NotificationBudget through NotificationRouter.apply_settings(), and the row key IS the class id lowercased (P1_critical → notify_p1_critical) so data/ui.json and data/notifications.json cannot drift. P4_ambient has no row because it has no channel — doc 08 ships it disabled and the budget refuses to enable it, so a row would be a switch that does nothing. Defaults mirror data/notifications.json's `default_enabled`; doc 12 §2.13's 'P3 off by default' is superseded, because C-71 made doc 08 sole owner of that answer and doc 08 says on.

doc 08 §2.13.3's explicit opt-in, default OFF: quiet hours otherwise defer even a P1 to the 08:00 summary. Informed rather than woken is the ship default, and this row is how a player who wants the 03:00 buzz asks for it.

PA-14 / doc 13 §2.7 step 6 — the row S10 never had. It is a STATE, not a preference: Android owns the answer, this app only reports it and offers the one action that is legal in each state (`off` -> ask; `blocked` -> open the app's page in system settings; `on`/`unavailable` -> nothing, and the row says so instead of pretending to be a switch). Hence `kind: state`, which stores the token PermissionFlow.settings_row_state() returns rather than a player's choice: it is NOT captured into a save and NOT in device_scoped_keys, because a value the platform re-reports every time it is looked at has nothing to persist. The four options ARE the four tokens, so a state this app could not render can never reach the row.

retired_rows._comment: PA-59, Wave 18 — WITHDRAWN from the sheet, kept here on purpose. §2.13 phrases this one as `never spend emergency contractor funds (on)`; the row was phrased as the sim key instead (spending ON/OFF) because an inverted control is the easiest settings bug to ship. Neither phrasing was the problem: `grep -rn auto_spend_contractor sim/ game/ ui/` finds no reader at all — `dispatch_policy.gd` stores the flag and there is no contractor unit to hire, which doc 06 line 1749 says outright. A control the sim never consults is a control that lies about what the player just did, so the ROW goes and the KEY stays: doc 06's `data/dispatch.json.policy_defaults` still carries it, `DispatchPolicy` still round-trips it, and a save written while the row existed still restores without a drop (`SettingsModel.retired_keys`). The row comes back the day a contractor unit does — restore this object to `rows` and nothing else changes.

save_slots._comment: S0/S9 Data & Saves. game/save_service.gd owns the files and the meta shape {slot, saved_at_unix, day_index, population, treasury}; this block owns only how many slots the player sees and which one autosave owns.

pause_menu._comment: Single-scene game: QUIT saves first and then closes the app, so `quit` is an intent the shell fulfils, never a bare get_tree().quit() from a view.

title._comment: S0, the front door (doc 12 §2.2). Shown at boot BEFORE the city; CONTINUE restores the newest save, NEW CITY founds one, SETTINGS opens S9 over the title. The shell owns every file operation — ui/title_model.gd reads slot meta through game/save_service.gd's published list_slots/latest_slot and writes nothing.
title._skyline_comment: The brand mark, in tools/gen_icon.py's own SKYLINE coordinate system: x grows right in the same units as y, y = 0 is the top of the tallest spire and ground_y is the street. These rows ARE the generator's TOWERS table, so the front door, the launcher icon and the boot splash are one drawing. The launcher crops five towers around the hero; the title shows all fifteen (doc 11's flagship rule — show the tall skyline).
title._palette_comment: 'Blackout blue' — the icon's own brand ramp, NOT the data-state palette. Mirrors tools/gen_icon.py's SKY_TOP / SKY_HORIZON / GROUND / SILHOUETTE / WINDOW_DARK / AMBER / AMBER_CORE / WORDMARK / TAGLINE. A colourblind variant does not touch it: it is a picture of a city at night, not a reading of city data (A6 governs the four data states).

veil._comment: S15, the loading veil (doc 12 §2.20, doc 13 §2.9/§2.9.1). `min_steps` is doc 13's own `catchup_veil_min_steps`: an offline catch-up worth fewer steps than this is sub-frame work and gets no veil, because a veil that flashes for one frame is a defect rather than a courtesy. A stepped RESTORE always gets one whatever its step count — its eleven steps run 0.2 ms to 76.5 ms, so few steps does not mean fast.

camera._comment: Interaction range only (C-63). Projection constants fov_deg/near_m/far_m live in data/render.json (doc 11) and are read from there; they must never be added to this block.
camera._pitch_manual: Wave 17 (doc 98 §43). The MANUAL pitch axis on top of pitch(t). pitch_manual_min_deg is the grazing floor the slider's TOP reaches (look up the facades — the user's complaint); pitch_manual_max_deg the top-down ceiling at the bottom. Composition is a normalised lean: pitch = lerp(curve(t), target, |bias| · reach(t)), so bias 0 is EXACTLY the curve's own answer at every zoom and the slider's middle detent is honest. 12° and not 10°: at 10° a D_MIN pose puts the camera 3.1 m up, inside the 3.5 m ground floor of doc 11 §2.6's shortest archetype; 18·sin12° = 3.74 m clears it, and the two degrees cost nothing on the read. 78° and not 90°: at 90° yaw stops meaning anything and the twist gesture becomes a spin about nothing.
camera._pitch_reach: The zoom coupling doc 92 §47 measured (report 98 RR-115). reach 1.0 means the whole authored band is reachable at that zoom; below 1.0 the slider's ends buy proportionally fewer degrees and the control's track visibly compresses rather than silently clamping. Interpolated by smoothstep(zoom_t) — the same shape the pitch curve itself opens on. The UP reach is the one the budget bites, and it bites at ONE angle: pitch = half the 40° FOV = 20° is where the horizon enters the top of the frame and the whole city enters the frustum with it. On the 1,500-building bench city, balanced, 1920x1080, by DAY (sun shadows on; night is cheaper in every cell), Z2 at a 12° floor measures 330 dc / 355 with the UI's 25, against the 320 budget, and its chunk census shows 4 NEAR chunks where the 62° curve has none — 420·sin 12° = 87 m is under doc 11 §2.5's 150 m NEAR boundary, so a lean alone re-tiers chunks into the shadow pass. 0.76 puts the far floor at 62 − 50·0.76 = 24°, i.e. 420·sin 24° = 171 m up, past that boundary: 233 dc / 258 with the UI, NEAR back to 0. Close in the whole band stays, and it is not free: the Z0 day floor measures 338 dc / 363 (+13 % over budget) and the Z1 floor 308 / 333. That excess is published rather than hidden (doc 92 §47, ruling 93 §AC2) because the pose that pays it is the one this axis exists for — look UP the facades — and because no band that shows the horizon at all can avoid it: the cliff is at 20°, not at the floor. The runtime guard is doc 11 §2.13's governor. Re-open: a Fold capture at a Z0/Z1 floor pose over 16.7 ms p95 at balanced lowers pitch_reach_up_near, or grows this row a mid knot. The DOWN reach costs nothing anywhere (Z2 at 78° is 164 dc) and stays 1.0.
camera._pitch_aim: Wave 18 (doc 98 §54, doc 12 §2.23.7, doc 93 §AM). THE AIM-HEIGHT RAMP, and the reason the pitch band alone did not do what it was built for. In this rig the camera looks AT THE FOCUS, and the focus is on the ground, so the horizon is always `pitch` ABOVE the view axis: at the 12° floor with a 40° FOV it sits (1 − tan12°/tan20°)/2 = 20.8 % down the frame and the ground owns the other 79 %. That is the 2026-09-02 complaint measured — a floor that is already grazing and still frames two-thirds pavement with the tower tops cropped off the TOP edge — and no floor fixes it, because 18·sin12° = 3.74 m is the last angle that clears doc 11 §2.6's 3.5 m ground floor. So the LOOK-AT point rises instead: look_at = focus + (0, aim, 0), aim = 0 at bias ≤ 0 (AUTO and the whole top-down half are bit-identical to the camera that shipped) and rising with the UP lean, scaled by the SAME reach(t) the pitch lean uses so the two halves of the axis can never disagree. aim_up_ground_frac is the share of the FRAME HEIGHT, from the bottom edge, the ground is left at a full lean: 1/3 is pavement in the bottom third, facades and sky above it, and it solves to aim = D·(sin p − cos p·tan v) with v = lerp(p, v_target, lean) and v_target = −atan((1 − 2·frac)·tan(fov/2)) = −6.92°. The LEAN interpolates the view ANGLE and the height is derived out of it, because scaling the full-lean height by the lean is not monotone — the orbit pitch is falling under the lean and takes R with it, so the Z0 aim peaks at 5.896 m near bias 0.95 and comes back to 5.879 m at bias 1, which the slider would show as the horizon nodding. At a full lean the height comes to 5.88 m at Z0, 23.1 m at the 0.42 default, 29.8 m at Z1 and 144.0 m at Z2. The lift is proportional to R and not a fixed number of metres BECAUSE THE RECOMPOSITION IS ANGULAR — a constant height would be a 74° pitch-up at Z0 and a rounding error at Z2. The authored 1/3 is checked against doc 02 rather than against taste: at the far pose (D 420, floor pitch 24°) it comes to 420·(sin24° + cos24°·tan20°/3) = 217.4 m, and doc 02 §2.3's five-rung roster maximum is high_rise L5 at 62 floors × doc 11's 3.5 m = 217.0 m — the same 217 m tower doc 11 §2.5 works its LOD example against. At full zoom-out the ramp aims at that roofline to within 0.4 m. §2.14's sixth rung (78 floors, 273 m) is deliberately not the scale: it is city-level gated growth stock, not the pose the far zoom is composed against. The camera POSITION does not move — a pure aim lift, so the ground-floor clearance, doc 11 §2.5's tiering and doc 92 §47.2's bought NEAR boundary all survive verbatim (doc 93 §AM1). aim_up_anchor_ndc is the one guard: the focus is the pan, pinch, twist and focus_on anchor and may not leave the frame, and it sits p − v below the axis, so the guard is v ≥ p − atan(ndc·tan(fov/2)). 1.0 puts it exactly on the bottom edge. It does NOT bind where the composition lives — Z0's full lean needs 12 + 6.92 = 18.92° of drop against the frame's 20° — and binds by 0.45° at Z1 and 3.5° at Z2, where reach has already shortened the lean for the budget's sake.
camera._pitch_feel: Mirrors the pan's gesture feel in bias units instead of metres: a 0.35 rubber band past either end while the finger is down, a closed-form fling on release, a critically damped return. pitch_detent_units is the middle detent's width — a release inside it lands on AUTO, which is how a player finds the middle without aiming at it.
camera._tilt_dp_per_unit: dp of vertical two-finger centroid travel for a FULL lean (bias 0 to ±1) in the two-finger tilt gesture (`TouchInput`). 260 dp is a comfortable two-finger stroke on a 400 dp landscape display, and it is about what the slider column gives when it has its authored 240 dp: the slider's own gain is its column (a full half-column is a full lean on that side), so the two axes agree wherever the column has room and the gesture is the one that keeps a fixed gain on a short display.
camera._tilt_slider: The right-edge control (doc 12 §2.23). One 48 dp touch column, vertically centred in the band left between the top bar and the bottom-right corner reservation — NOT in the whole safe area, because the incident drawer's handle keeps the edge from 60 to 220 dp above the bottom and a naively centred column lands on it at every landscape box. h_dp is what it takes when there is room, min_h_dp the floor below which it stands down entirely (D-16's rule: an affordance that has stood down costs the others nothing). fade_after_s and ghost_alpha are §2.23's resting state.

gestures_dp_ms._tilt: Wave 17. The two-finger TILT arm of the MULTI state. It engages on the same 24 dp of travel a pinch does, but only while the span has drifted less than HALF the pinch slop and the bearing less than half the twist deadzone — a gesture already on its way to a pinch or a twist can never be stolen by the tilt. tilt_dominance_ratio is the last discriminator: the centroid must be moving at least 1.5x further vertically than horizontally, which is what separates a tilt from a two-finger drag across the map.

placement._max_run_tiles: §2.7's drag-path tools (roads, water mains) commit ONE run as ONE command and ONE bill, so a stroke has to have an end. 48 tiles is three land blocks of frontage — long enough that no ordinary street or main is two commands, short enough that a thumb sliding off the display quotes $86,400 of street rather than $250,000 of avenue. It is a safety rail on the GESTURE and not a rule about roads: the player commits and sweeps again. `PathTool` truncates the far end of the L at this length, so the preview is always exactly the run the commit lays.

speed._comment_auto_speed_reset: PA-84, Wave 18 — WHICH critical. Doc 01 §2.9 and doc 12 §2.11 have said `resets speed to 1x on a critical event` since the first draft and `HudModel.auto_speed_reset` had no caller outside its own test, because `critical` was never defined and the obvious reading (every CRITICAL-state alert) would drop the player to 1x several times an hour under PA-07's alert load — a game that keeps taking the speed control away is worse than one that never had the feature. So the trigger set is authored here, it is THREE events, and each one is a thing the player cannot fix at 3x: an incident that ran out of time, the credit limit (spending is blocked until income recovers), and the flood band at which streets close. Each is doc 08's own P1 binding in data/notifications.json, spelled as the sim event rather than the notify_id so this list needs no notification config to read. `rearm_real_s` is 1800 -- THIRTY real minutes, not the ten PA-84 suggested, and the number is a measurement rather than a guess. tools/measure_speed_resets.gd over eleven seeds: at 600 s the worst seed (8888) forces 1.071 resets per real hour, which MISSES the audit's own <= 1 bar; at 1200 s the worst is 0.952; at 1800 s it is 0.714. The reason 600 s does not work is not burstiness -- seed 8888 has the FEWEST raw triggers of the eleven (41) and the MOST forced resets, because its crises are spread out, which is exactly the case a short re-arm cannot coalesce. Thirty real minutes is thirty game-hours at 1x, and it reads as a rule a player would accept: at most one forced speed reset per half-hour of play.

storm_prep._source: 12-ui-ux.md §2.24 (S17). Doc 07 §2.7.7 owns the six actions and their knobs; doc 03 owns their dollars (data/economy.json storm_prep); this block is layout only.

onboarding._comment: S12 (doc 12 §2.17) at the scope the shipped verbs support. The doc's eleven-step table assumes player-drawn power lines and water mains, a Land tab and a review-ledger beat; §2.17's own thesis sentence — 'one component fails, four other systems degrade, the player dispatches a finite crew, and the lights come back on' — is what this table teaches with the commands that exist today (cmd_place_building, cmd_place_grid_component, cmd_dispatch_unit, trigger_tutorial_transformer_failure). Steps the verbs cannot carry yet (confirm_water, review_ledger, service_building, upgrade, buy_land) are NOT renumbered or faked: they are absent, and adding one is a row here plus its string, never a code change.
onboarding._geometry: §2.17's coach-mark rendering, verbatim: dim #000000 @ 0.55, an 8 dp / 12 dp rounded cutout animated over layout.coach_cutout_anim_s, a bubble no wider than 240 dp, and copy capped at 90 characters so it reads in one glance.
onboarding._director: §2.17's global guarantee: the disaster director is suppressed for the whole tutorial and 300 real seconds after it, so the only incident that exists is the scripted one. The model REQUESTS both through its action queue; doc 07 owns the switch.
onboarding._region_radius: How much slack a `region` match allows, in tiles (Chebyshev). 1 keeps the marked lot the marked lot while forgiving a fat finger on the tile next to it.
onboarding._camera: Step 1 completes on observed CameraState movement — both verbs, because a player who only pans has not learnt to zoom. 48 m is six tiles; 0.05 zoom_t is a quarter of one double-tap step.

steps._advance_note: No `match` on the incident kind, on purpose: SimEventBus.emit stamps `type` with the EVENT name, so a bus event never carries doc 06's incident type. It does not need to — §2.17's global guarantee is that the director is suppressed and RNG spawning is off for the whole tutorial, so the only incident that can be created here is the scripted one.

steps._comment: The handoff (doc 09 §2.14). The tutorial used to end here and leave the player in a running city with nothing to aim at; this step points at the one surface that always knows what to do next. SOFT, and satisfied by either opening the sheet or acknowledging the card — a player who has understood does not need to be made to tap.

in_app_alerts._comment: FOREGROUND banners and toasts ONLY (C-71/C-72). These are ~3x doc 08's PUSH budgets in data/notifications.json and that is deliberate: an in-app banner costs a glance the player is already giving. Never read these to decide a push, or a push budget to decide a banner.
